name: Alexander Kraft
blurb: Monte Carlo tailoring: Savile Row structure — high armholes, nipped waist, working buttonholes — cut with Italian lightness. 1930s–40s Hollywood glamour meets 1960s Riviera ease; his own references are Agnelli, Niven and Cary Grant in To Catch a Thief.
signatureDesc: Navy blazer with cream trousers and brown loafers
rules: Fit is the whole game: coat sleeves, trouser break and waist suppression exact — details make an off-the-peg suit read bespoke.
A tie makes any suit — or slacks and a sports coat — infinitely more elegant. Open-necked by default is the uniform of men who stopped trying.
Away from the beach: long trousers in linen, cotton or light wool — cream, white or navy. Sockless, always; sandals, never.
avoid: Avoid: logos, trends copied slavishly, and cheap quantity — quality is remembered long after price is forgotten.

name: Alessandro Squarzi
blurb: Milan's vintage archivist, founder of Fortela. American military and Western wear, Japanese selvedge denim and Italian tailoring worn as one wardrobe — sprezzatura that comes from clothes genuinely lived in, never styled to look that way.
signatureDesc: Indigo denim jacket with white jeans and brown loafers
rules: Never more than three colours: navy, olive, white, brown — earth tones carry the look, one accent at most.
Worn-in beats box-fresh. Vintage drapes better and reads honest; new pieces should be built to be kept for years, not seasons.
Anchor workwear with one dressed piece — Oxfords with white denim, a tailored jacket over a Western shirt. The friction is the style.
avoid: Avoid: head-to-toe newness, fast fashion, and anything worn for anyone but yourself.

name: Gianni Agnelli
blurb: L'Avvocato. Grey flannel, unlined shoulders and rustic shoes with boardroom suits — the original lesson that you must master the rules completely before you're allowed to break exactly one of them, on purpose, every time.
signatureDesc: Charcoal blazer with grey trousers and brown boots
rules: Master the rule first, then break one — watch over the cuff, boots with a suit. One deviation is sprezzatura; three is carelessness.
Grey flannel and navy are a complete wardrobe. Texture does the talking so colour doesn't have to.
Everything slightly undone, nothing actually sloppy: the collar open, the tailoring immaculate.
avoid: Avoid: trying to look effortless. Agnelli's ease was rehearsed for decades — earn yours the same way.

name: Cary Grant
blurb: The best-dressed man of the twentieth century by accumulation of restraint: mid-grey suits, high collars chosen to flatter his neck, nothing ever quite new-looking. His father sold suits; Grant's lesson is that elegance is subtraction.
signatureDesc: Grey blazer with light blue shirt and navy trousers
rules: Dress to camouflage your flaws and repeat what flatters you — Grant's high collars hid a thick neck for fifty years.
Mid-grey is the most useful colour a man owns: it takes white, blue, navy and brown without argument.
Never look brand new. Clothes should appear to have been yours for years, because the good ones will be.
avoid: Avoid: novelty. Grant wore essentially one look for five decades and never repeated the mistake of changing it.
shoeDetail: dark brown, polished but not gleaming

name: Ralph Lauren
blurb: Tweed over denim, the cricket sweater, the polo coat — English country cloth cut through American sport. Lauren's engine is layering: three honest textures in one look, each from a different tradition, none of them fighting.
signatureDesc: Cream cricket sweater with indigo jeans and brown loafers
rules: Layer across traditions: country tweed, American denim, a sporting knit. One look, three textures, zero conflict.
Heritage colours only — cream, forest, navy, camel, burgundy. If it wouldn't appear on a 1930s clubhouse wall, leave it out.
Romance is a styling tool: clothes should suggest a life being lived, not a product being launched.
avoid: Avoid: single-note outfits. A Lauren look with nothing layered is just clothes.

name: Gerardo Cavaliere
blurb: Salerno-born, raised on the Amalfi Coast — a lawyer who left the law for the cutting table. His Sartoria Giuliva tailoring is made to bespoke level in Naples and fitted by him in Rome; with his wife Margherita Cardelli he co-founded Giuliva Heritage to carry that Neapolitan hand into ready-to-wear. Tradition held firmly, then coloured with experiment.
signatureDesc: Navy blazer with burgundy knit and cream trousers
rules: Generous, never tight: wider lapels, a longer jacket, high-rise trousers harmonious from waist to hem — Neapolitan ease is cut in, not squeezed out.
Hold the tradition, then colour it: master the classic rules first, then experiment with shape, weight and geometry until the formality softens.
Layer by hand and history: a fine knit or a scarf under tailoring, vintage cloth over new — style is the footprint of what you are, not a trend you followed.
avoid: Avoid: skinny cuts, stiff construction, and dressing by trend — Cavaliere never followed one, and the clothes show it.

name: David Beckham
blurb: The footballer who became British menswear's ambassador. As a partner in Kent & Curwen he modernised its sporting heritage — cricket jumpers, rugby shirts, flat caps — while his own tailoring sharpened into double-breasted and three-piece suits with a Savile Row nod. Equally precise in a leather jacket and boots; the constants are fit, grooming and detail.
signatureDesc: Charcoal blazer with white shirt, indigo jeans and brown boots
rules: Fit is the signature: tailoring cut close and clean, basics fitted the same way — if it doesn't fit, it isn't finished.
Heritage with a modern twist: British sporting cloth — check, tweed, the cricket jumper, the flat cap — updated for now, never worn as costume.
Dress the whole man: pocket square, grooming, the right watch — his detail runs from the socks to the velvet jacket, nothing left to chance.
avoid: Avoid: the early-2000s experiments — the sarong-era novelty is the one chapter even Beckham left behind.
shoeDetail: dark brown Chelsea boots, fresh pair

name: Tom Ford
blurb: After a decade reshaping Gucci and Yves Saint Laurent, Ford launched his own house in 2005 on a single idea: tailoring as architecture. Wide peak lapels, roped shoulders, high armholes and a dramatically suppressed waist — the Shelton and O'Connor silhouette he put on Daniel Craig's Bond from Quantum of Solace onward. Evening is his home ground: velvet dinner jackets and shawl collars in midnight blue.
signatureDesc: Burgundy blazer with white shirt and black trousers
rules: Build the V: strong roped shoulder, wide peak lapel, suppressed waist. Ford's jacket is structure first — the silhouette is the statement.
Better overdressed than underdressed: a crisp white poplin shirt with any dark suit, and every detail finished — collar, pocket square, shine on the shoe.
After dark, commit: velvet or a shawl collar, midnight blue over black, one statement piece and everything else plain.
avoid: Avoid: skinny modern cuts, notch lapels on a tuxedo, and loafers under black tie — Ford's rules are not suggestions.
